content: Hydrogen chloride (HCl) is a chemical compound with the molecular formula HCl. At room temperature, it exists as a colorless gas. When exposed to atmospheric moisture, it forms white fumes of hydrochloric acid. Both hydrogen chloride gas and hydrochloric acid are of significant importance in various technological and industrial applications. The term HCl is often used to refer to hydrochloric acid, which is an aqueous solution derived from hydrogen chloride gas. From a chemical perspective, hydrogen chloride consists of diatomic molecules, each containing one hydrogen atom (H) and one chlorine atom (Cl) connected by a covalent single bond. Due to the high electronegativity of chlorine compared to hydrogen, the bond is highly polar, resulting in a significant dipole moment. The chlorine atom carries a partial negative charge (δ-), while the hydrogen atom carries a partial positive charge (δ+). This polarity makes HCl highly soluble in water and other polar solvents. When dissolved in water, HCl reacts to form hydronium ions (H₃O⁺) and chloride ions (Cl⁻) in a reversible reaction, producing hydrochloric acid, which is classified as a strong acid. The acid dissociation constant (Ka) of HCl is large, indicating nearly complete ionization in water. Even in the absence of water, hydrogen chloride can act as an acid, dissolving in other solvents like methanol and protonating molecules or ions. It can also serve as an acid catalyst in chemical reactions under anhydrous conditions. Hydrogen chloride is a corrosive gas, particularly in the presence of moisture. Its acidic nature allows it to protonate methanol (CH₃OH) molecules, and it can cause severe damage to tissues upon contact. When inhaled, hydrogen chloride fumes can irritate the respiratory tract, causing coughing, choking, and inflammation of the nose, throat, and upper respiratory system. In severe cases, it can lead to pulmonary edema, circulatory failure, or even death. Skin contact with hydrogen chloride can result in redness, pain, and severe burns, while exposure to the eyes can cause permanent damage. Historically, alchemists in the Middle Ages recognized hydrochloric acid (then known as spirit of salt or acidum salis) as a source of hydrogen chloride gas, which they referred to as marine acid air. In the 17th century, Johann Rudolf Glauber prepared hydrogen chloride by reacting sodium chloride (salt) with sulfuric acid, a process later reported by Carl Wilhelm Scheele in 1772. Joseph Priestley also prepared hydrogen chloride in the same year, and in 1810, Humphry Davy confirmed that it was composed of hydrogen and chlorine. During the Industrial Revolution, the demand for alkaline substances like soda ash led to the development of the Leblanc process, which produced hydrogen chloride as a by-product. Initially, this gas was released into the atmosphere, but the Alkali Act of 1863 mandated its absorption into water to produce hydrochloric acid on an industrial scale. The Leblanc process was eventually replaced by the Solvay process in the early 20th century, which did not produce hydrogen chloride. However, hydrogen chloride production continued as a step in hydrochloric acid manufacturing. In the 20th century, hydrogen chloride was used in the production of chlorinated monomers like chloroprene and vinyl chloride, which are polymerized to produce materials such as polychloroprene (Neoprene) and polyvinyl chloride (PVC). For example, in the production of vinyl chloride, hydrogen chloride is added across the triple bond of acetylene (C₂H₂), converting it into a double bond and yielding vinyl chloride. The acetylene process for making chloroprene involved joining two acetylene molecules and adding hydrogen chloride to the intermediate product. This process was later replaced by a method that adds chlorine (Cl₂) to 1,3-butadiene, with subsequent elimination reactions producing hydrogen chloride and chloroprene. Most industrially produced hydrogen chloride is used to manufacture hydrochloric acid. In the chlor-alkali industry, salt solutions are electrolyzed to produce chlorine gas (Cl₂), sodium hydroxide, and hydrogen gas (H₂). The chlorine gas can be recombined with hydrogen to form hydrogen chloride gas in an exothermic reaction, often carried out in an HCl oven. The resulting hydrogen chloride gas is absorbed into deionized water to produce chemically pure hydrochloric acid, which is used in various applications, including the food industry. In laboratory settings, small amounts of hydrogen chloride gas can be generated by dehydrating hydrochloric acid. This can be achieved by adding sulfuric acid or anhydrous calcium chloride to concentrated hydrochloric acid. Alternatively, hydrogen chloride can be produced by reacting sulfuric acid with sodium chloride. This method is sometimes used in clandestine laboratories to convert freebase drugs into their hydrochloride salts for easier distribution. Hydrogen chloride can also be prepared by hydrolyzing reactive chloride compounds such as phosphorus chlorides, thionyl chloride (SOCl₂), or acyl chlorides. For example, dripping cold water onto phosphorus pentachloride (PCl₅) produces hydrogen chloride gas, while hot water can hydrolyze PCl₅ further to form orthophosphoric acid. Similarly, the reaction of water with phosphorus trichloride (PCl₃) or thionyl chloride yields hydrogen chloride gas. Hydrogen chloride has numerous applications, including its use in the production of hydrochloric acid, the hydrochlorination of rubber, and the manufacture of vinyl and alkyl chlorides. It serves as a chemical intermediate in various industrial processes and is used in products like toilet bowl cleaners and as a flux in babbitting. It is also employed in the semiconductor industry for etching crystals and converting silicon to trichlorosilane (SiHCl₃) for silicon purification. Hydrogen chloride is typically stored in compressed gas cylinders, which are either red and brown or gray with a yellow band.
